title: Atomic Packing and Crystal Lattices
description: How atoms arrange themselves — and why it matters

concepts.title: Three Common Metallic Structures
concepts.contentHtml:
Most pure metals adopt one of three densely packed crystal structures:

  • Face-Centred Cubic (FCC) — atoms at corners and face centres of a cube. Coordination number 12, packing efficiency 74 %. Examples: Cu, Al, Au, Ag, γ-Fe.
  • Body-Centred Cubic (BCC) — atoms at corners plus one in the centre. Coordination 8, packing efficiency 68 %. Examples: α-Fe, Cr, W, Mo, Nb.
  • Hexagonal Close-Packed (HCP) — alternating ABAB layers of close-packed planes. Coordination 12, packing efficiency 74 %. Examples: Mg, Zn, Ti, Zr.

FCC and HCP both achieve the maximum possible packing density for spheres of equal size — they differ only in how the close-packed planes stack (ABCABC for FCC, ABAB for HCP).
mathExpressions: APF = \frac{\text{volume of atoms in unit cell}}{\text{volume of unit cell}}

concepts.title: Why Structure Controls Properties
concepts.contentHtml:
The crystal structure dictates many bulk properties:

  • Ductility: FCC metals (copper, aluminium, austenitic stainless) are very ductile because they have many close-packed slip planes available. HCP metals are less ductile — fewer accessible slip systems. BCC sits in between.
  • Density: FCC and HCP are denser than BCC for the same atom (same APF, but BCC is looser).
  • Magnetic and electronic behaviour: BCC α-Fe is ferromagnetic (up to its Curie point, 770 °C), while FCC γ-Fe, stable above 912 °C, is not. Same atoms, different lattice — different physics.

'Materials science' begins with this insight: chemistry tells you what the atoms are; structure tells you how they sit together; properties emerge from both.

concepts.title: Beyond Pure Metals
concepts.contentHtml:
Other classes of materials use different lattice families:

  • Ionic crystals — NaCl (rock salt structure), CsCl (CsCl-type), CaF₂ (fluorite). Cation/anion size ratio dictates the structure.
  • Covalent networks — diamond cubic (Si, Ge, C-diamond), wurtzite (ZnO, GaN). Each atom has four tetrahedral neighbours.
  • Perovskite — ABX₃, the family that produced superconductors, ferroelectrics like BaTiO₃, and modern lead-halide solar cells.
  • Molecular crystals — held together by van der Waals or hydrogen bonds, e.g. ice, naphthalene.

X-ray diffraction is the standard technique for determining all of these structures: every crystal produces a unique reciprocal-space fingerprint via Bragg's law nλ = 2d sin θ.

concepts.title: The 14 Bravais Lattices
concepts.contentHtml:
Auguste Bravais (1850) showed there are exactly 14 distinct three-dimensional lattices consistent with crystalline periodicity. They are organised into seven crystal systems (cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, hexagonal, trigonal, monoclinic, triclinic) and four centring types (primitive P, body-centred I, face-centred F, base-centred C).

Combining these gives the 14 Bravais types — for example, cubic admits P, I, and F variants (simple cubic, BCC, FCC), but not C-centred cubic, because that arrangement is geometrically equivalent to a smaller primitive lattice.

Every periodic crystal in nature, no matter how complicated its basis of atoms, sits on one of these 14 lattices. They are the most fundamental classification in solid-state science.

concepts.title: Miller Indices for Planes
concepts.contentHtml:
Crystal planes are labelled with three integers (hkl) called Miller indices. To find them:

  1. Find where the plane intercepts the three crystal axes, in units of the unit cell edges (a, b, c).
  2. Take the reciprocals of those intercepts.
  3. Clear fractions to give the smallest integers.

Example: a plane intersecting the axes at (1, ½, ∞) has reciprocals (1, 2, 0), giving Miller indices (120). The notation (100), (110), and (111) refers to the simplest cube-face, edge-bisecting, and corner-cutting planes respectively.

Miller indices appear in slip systems, X-ray diffraction conditions, surface energy tables — virtually every quantitative aspect of crystal physics.

concepts.title: Slip Systems and Anisotropy
concepts.contentHtml:
A slip system is a combination of a close-packed plane (where dislocations move) and a close-packed direction within it. The number of independent slip systems controls plastic flow:

  • FCC — 12 active slip systems (close-packed {111} planes, <110> directions). Highly ductile.
  • BCC — many planes available, but slip is harder; ductility is high above the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature.
  • HCP — only the basal {0001} plane is normally active, giving few independent systems and limited ductility at room temperature.

This is why oxygen-free copper (FCC) wraps cleanly around a former, while a magnesium ingot (HCP) is much harder to roll without cracking.

concepts.title: Why Defects Are Inevitable
concepts.contentHtml:
A perfect crystal is a useful idealisation, but no real crystal at finite temperature is perfect. Thermodynamics requires defects: removing atoms from lattice sites raises internal energy by some fixed cost ΔH_v, but the configurational entropy gained is enormous. The free-energy minimum sits at a non-zero defect concentration:

n_v / N ≈ exp(−ΔH_v / k_B T)

For copper near melting point, roughly 1 atom in 10,000 is a vacancy. Lower temperatures freeze in fewer defects but never zero. Properties from electrical resistivity to diffusion are dominated by the defect concentrations actually present, not by some idealised perfect crystal.

concepts.title: Vacancies, Interstitials, and Substitutions
concepts.contentHtml:
The three classical point defects:

  • Vacancy — a lattice site where an atom is missing.
  • Interstitial — an atom squeezed into a gap between normal lattice sites. Self-interstitials cost a lot of strain energy; small foreign atoms (H, C, N, O) interstitially in metals are common and important — carbon-in-iron is the basis of all steel.
  • Substitutional — a foreign atom replacing a host atom on its lattice site. Brass is Zn substituting on Cu sites; bronze is Sn on Cu.

Ionic crystals must keep charge balance, leading to paired defects:

  • Schottky pair — a cation vacancy plus an anion vacancy.
  • Frenkel pair — an ion displaced from its site to an interstitial position, leaving a vacancy behind.

concepts.title: Diffusion and Properties
concepts.contentHtml:
Atoms move through solids primarily by hopping into vacancies. The diffusion coefficient is set by an Arrhenius law:

D = D₀ exp(−Q / k_B T)

where Q is the activation energy for atomic jumps. Doubling temperature near a phase boundary can change diffusion rates by orders of magnitude, which is why heat treatment is so powerful: a few hours at 700 °C can homogenise a casting that would take geological time to even out at room temperature.

Point defects also dominate:

  • Electrical resistivity in metals — each impurity scatters electrons.
  • Coloration of crystals — F-centres in halides, Cr³⁺ on Al³⁺ sites in corundum producing rubies.
  • Doping in semiconductors — a single substitutional atom per million can control conductivity (boron in silicon, phosphorus in silicon).

title: Dislocations
description: The line defects that explain plastic flow

concepts.title: Why Real Metals Are So Soft
concepts.contentHtml:
If you calculate the stress required to slide one perfect crystal plane over another by simultaneously breaking every bond, you get a value roughly G/10, where G is the shear modulus. For copper that is about 5 GPa.

But real copper yields at a few tens of MPa — about 100 to 1000 times less than the ideal calculation. Why?

The answer, proposed independently by Taylor, Orowan, and Polanyi in 1934, is that crystals contain dislocations: line defects that move under modest stress, sliding one crystal plane over another a single bond at a time, like a caterpillar moving by propagating a hump. You don't have to break every bond at once; only the bond at the dislocation core.

Dislocations were not directly observed until transmission electron microscopy in the 1950s confirmed Taylor's hypothesis.

concepts.title: Edge and Screw Dislocations
concepts.contentHtml:
Two pure types:

  • Edge dislocation — an extra half-plane of atoms inserted into the crystal. Its boundary is the dislocation line. The Burgers vector b (the slip increment per dislocation) is perpendicular to the line.
  • Screw dislocation — a helical ramp of atomic planes spiralling around an axis. The Burgers vector is parallel to the line.

Real dislocation loops are usually mixed, with edge and screw character varying along the loop. The Burgers vector remains constant along the line.

Slip occurs by dislocation motion: the line glides through the crystal, and one Burgers vector of slip is added each time it sweeps from one side to the other. The resulting plastic strain is permanent.

concepts.title: Strengthening Mechanisms
concepts.contentHtml:
Engineering metals are strong precisely because their dislocations are obstructed. Common strengthening mechanisms:

  • Strain hardening (work hardening) — plastic deformation multiplies dislocations until they tangle and obstruct each other. Cold-rolled copper is much stronger than annealed copper.
  • Solid-solution strengthening — substitutional or interstitial atoms locally distort the lattice and create stress fields dislocations must overcome.
  • Grain-size strengthening (Hall-Petch) — grain boundaries block dislocation motion. Yield stress scales as σ_y = σ_0 + k/√d, where d is grain size.
  • Precipitation hardening — fine second-phase particles (e.g. Mg-Zn-rich precipitates in 7075 aluminium) pin dislocations.
  • Phase transformations — martensitic transformations distort the lattice into a hard, defective structure (heat-treated steel).

Heat treatment, alloying, and forging are all about controlling the dislocation population and the obstacles it faces.

title: Surface and Volume Defects
description: Grain boundaries, twins, and pores — defects beyond the line

concepts.title: Grain Boundaries
concepts.contentHtml:
Most engineering metals are polycrystalline: aggregates of small (typically 1–100 µm) crystallites — grains — each with a different orientation. Where two grains meet, the lattice cannot match perfectly. The thin (a few atoms wide) misfit region is a grain boundary, and it has its own excess free energy γ_GB ~ 0.5–1 J/m².

Grain boundaries:

  • Block dislocation motion (Hall-Petch strengthening).
  • Provide fast diffusion paths along the boundary plane.
  • Are favoured sites for second-phase precipitation, segregation of impurities, and the start of corrosion or fracture.

Heat treatment that grows grains (annealing) can soften a metal by reducing total grain boundary area; the reverse — keeping grains small — strengthens it.

concepts.title: Twins and Stacking Faults
concepts.contentHtml:
Special low-energy planar defects:

  • Twin boundaries — a mirror-symmetric switch in stacking. Annealing twins in copper and brass are familiar; deformation twins are an alternative to slip in metals with limited slip systems (HCP titanium, magnesium, zinc).
  • Stacking faults — a local error in the layer sequence (e.g. ABCBCABC instead of ABCABC). The energy γ_SF varies between materials and controls how easily dislocations split into partial dislocations.

Stacking-fault energy is one of the parameters that determines whether an FCC metal preferentially deforms by slip (high γ_SF, like aluminium) or by twinning (low γ_SF, like silver and TWIP steels) — and therefore how it work-hardens.

concepts.title: Pores, Inclusions, and Hierarchical Defects
concepts.contentHtml:
Real materials also contain three-dimensional defects:

  • Pores and voids — gas bubbles trapped during solidification, or shrinkage cavities. Concentrate stress and act as fatigue crack initiators.
  • Inclusions — embedded second-phase particles (oxides, sulphides). Large inclusions in steels are notorious starting points for fatigue failure.
  • Cracks — already-formed planes of separation, the topic of fracture mechanics.

Modern materials engineering treats defects on every length scale at once: point defects (atomic), dislocations (nanometre), grain boundaries and twins (micrometre), pores and inclusions (tens of micrometres), and macroscopic cracks. Performance is dominated by the most critical defect at the relevant length scale — often a single inclusion or pore can determine the strength of an entire forging.
